“Banjo” Dan Linder Brings Vt. Songs to Aldrich Library
Dan Lindner, a/k/a “Banjo Dan,” will discuss and perform songs based on Vermont events, people, and stories at the Aldrich Public Library, 6 Washington St., Barre, on Wednesday, May 6, 2026, at 1:30 p.m. Dan’s program is part of the library’s ongoing “Senior Day” series which the Friends of the Library support. Free and open to all ages, the May 6 concert will be specially dedicated to the memory of late Friends president, Christine Litchfield.
During a musical career spanning fifty years, ”Banjo Dan” has written nearly four hundred songs in the folk/bluegrass/country genre, recording over one hundred of them in an extensive catalog of albums under his own name and those of groups he has performed with, most notably Banjo Dan and the Mid-nite Plowboys. His four volume series of “Banjo Dan’s Songs of Vermont” features an array of Vermont themes, many inspired by legend and lore as well as historical events, while his recently released “Spirits” album offers a collection of songs inspired by an array of spiritual concepts and traditions.
Lindner will recount the stories behind some of his Vermont songs and discuss and illustrate the ways he has sought to effectively deliver these tales in music. The presentation will feature live performances of a number of his original Vermont songs.
Refreshments by the Friends will be served after the concert when the winner of the Friends’ annual gardening raffle will be drawn. Raffle items include a trowel, potting soil, seeds, gloves, a $25 gift certificate to Aubuchon Hardware, and much more. Tickets for the raffle are still available at the library ($1 for 1 and $5 for 6) until May 6.
—
Waterbury Public Library
Poems By Heart
In celebration of National Poetry Month, join four Vermont-based writers as they read from their work at the Waterbury Public Library on Wednesday, April 29 from 6:30-8 p.m. in the Library’s SAL Room in “Poems by Heart” with a nod to Rainer Maria Rilke: "It is spring again. The earth is like a child that knows poems by heart." Writers include Burlington's Alison Prine, Waitsfield's Erika Nichols-Frazer, Waterbury's Colleen Ovelman, and Fayston's Helen Whybrow who will explore the themes of spring, including birth, loss, and renewal.
Alison Prine’s latest collection of poems, "Loss and Its Antonym" (Headmistress Press, 2024), won the Sappho’s Prize in Poetry and was a finalist for the Vermont Book Award. Her debut poetry collection, STEEL (Cider Press Review, 2016), was also named a finalist for the Vermont Book Award. Her poems have appeared in Ploughshares, The Virginia Quarterly Review, Five Points, Harvard Review, Prairie Schooner, and others. She lives and works in Burlington, Vermont. Visit her at alisonprine.com.
Erika Nichols-Frazer is the author of the poetry collection "Staring Too Closely" and the memoir "Feed Me: A Story of Food, Love and Mental Illness", as well as the forthcoming poetry chapbook "Can you see her, the moon?" coming out from Finishing Line Press in June 2026 and the short story collection "No One Will Ever Hear You", coming out from Rootstock Publishing in September 2026. She has an MFA from the Bennington Writing Seminars and has published more than 30 short stories, poems, and essays in literary journals such as "River Teeth's Beautiful Things", "Emerge Literary Journal", "Gone Lawn", and others. She works at Vermont State University and lives in Waitsfield with her husband, infant daughter, and various animals.
Colleen Ovelman's creative work has appeared in "Best of the Burlington Writer’s Workshop", "Grand Exit" podcast, "Vermont Stage’s Winter Tales", "Philadelphia Stories", and elsewhere. She has been awarded fellowships and residencies from the Vermont Studio Center and Hollowdeck Press's Poet Cottage. She is working on a collection of poems, a history of mending, which explores living with grief in the aftermath of her teenage son's death. Her son, Eli, was killed along with four of his friends from the Mad River Valley in 2016. Colleen lives with her family in Waterbury, Vermont.
Helen Whybrow is a writer, editor and organic farmer whose book about shepherding, land and belonging, "The Salt Stones", was longlisted for the National Book Award and chosen as a New Yorker Best Book of 2025. Her other titles include "Dead Reckoning" (W. W. Norton, 2001) and "A Man Apart" (Chelsea Green, 2015). She has a master’s in journalism and has taught writing at Middlebury College and the Breadloaf Environmental Writer’s Conference. She and her family farm and steward a refuge for land justice at Knoll Farm in Fayston, Vermont.
No registration is required, simply drop-in. Q&A at the end with light refreshments.
